title: Malignant neuroleptic syndrome following deep brain stimulation surgery: a case report
case_prompt: A 54-year-old man with a 14-year history of Parkinson’s disease (PD) was admitted for bilateral subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation (DBS). His regimen consisted of levodopa 600 mg/day, carbidopa 125 mg/day, entacapone 1200 mg/day, and pramipexole 0.54 mg/day, all of which were discontinued 18 hours before surgery to optimize intraoperative testing. The DBS electrodes were placed uneventfully. Three hours postoperatively, he developed tremor, muscle rigidity, and a fever unresponsive to acetaminophen. Clinicians initially attributed these findings to PD and administered levodopa 200 mg three times daily via a nasogastric tube. Systemic and central nervous system infection were considered, but cerebrospinal fluid analysis, chest radiography, and blood and urine cultures were normal. Brain MRI showed no intracranial pathology and confirmed optimal lead placement. Twelve hours after surgery, he exhibited severe axial and appendicular rigidity, a coarse resting tremor, prolonged spasms of the extremities, a temperature of 40 °C, and blood pressure of 165/94 mmHg. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 19.4 × 10^9/L with left shift, a creatine kinase level of 1500 U/L with a normal CK-MB fraction, and normal cardiac troponin levels.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Parkinson’s disease exacerbation — “The tremor and rigidity were attributed to PD and 200 mg levodopa three times daily was administered through a nasogastric tube.”  
2. Systemic and central nervous system infection — “Systemic and central nervous system infection were also considered in the differential diagnosis; however, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, a chest X-ray, and blood and urine cultures were all within normal limits.”  
3. Intracranial pathology or lead misplacement — “A subsequent brain magnetic resonance imaging scan depicted no intracranial pathology and confirmed optimal lead placement.”  
4. Malignant hyperthermia — “Malignant hyperthermia was excluded after a negative caffeine-halothane contracture test.”
